questions.q: Define "creep" in the context of mass movement and state one visible field indicator of its occurrence.
questions.a: Creep is the imperceptibly slow, continuous downslope movement of soil and regolith under gravity, typically <1 cm/year. A visible indicator is curved tree trunks (pistol-butt trees) or tilted fence posts/telephone poles. A wrong answer (e.g., "fast movement of mud") reveals confusion with mudflow/earthflow and inability to recognise the timescale distinction.

questions.q: Explain why earthflows are more common in humid regions with thick clay-rich regolith, whereas landslides dominate in steep, jointed bedrock areas like the Himalayas.
questions.a: Earthflows require fine-grained, water-saturated material that behaves viscously; humid climates provide sustained moisture, and clay-rich regolith (from chemical weathering) supplies the material. Landslides need coherent rock masses that fail along discrete planes; steep, tectonically jointed bedrock in the Himalayas provides such planes. A wrong answer (e.g., "earthflows happen only in deserts") shows failure to link material properties, climate, and movement mechanics.

questions.q: A slope in the Western Ghats has a 30° gradient, deep lateritic soil, and receives 3000 mm annual rainfall. After a cloudburst, a 2 m thick layer of saturated soil moves 50 m downslope in 10 minutes as a chaotic, fluid mass. Classify this mass movement and justify using three diagnostic criteria.
questions.a: Classification: Mudflow. Justification: (1) High water content (saturated soil, cloudburst) → fluid behaviour. (2) Velocity ~30 m/h (50 m in 10 min) → rapid, not slow like earthflow/creep. (3) Material: fine-grained lateritic soil, not coherent rock blocks → excludes landslide. A wrong classification (e.g., "landslide") indicates overlooking water content and material texture as discriminators.

questions.q: Compare the spatial distribution of "Very High Vulnerability" landslide zones in the Himalayas versus the Western Ghats using the controlling factors: geology, slope, rainfall, and human activity.
questions.a: Himalayas: young, tectonically active, jointed sedimentary/metamorphic rocks; very steep slopes; high seismicity; intense monsoon rainfall; heavy construction (roads, dams). Western Ghats: old, weathered basalt/ laterite; steep escarpments; extremely high orographic rainfall; deforestation/plantation agriculture. Both share steep slopes and high rainfall, but Himalayas add seismic shaking and weaker rock structure, while Ghats add deep weathering profiles. A wrong answer (e.g., "only rainfall matters") misses the multi-factor interplay.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Afforestation alone can eliminate landslide risk in the Himalayas." Provide two supporting and two limiting arguments.
questions.a: Supporting: (1) Roots increase soil cohesion and shear strength. (2) Vegetation intercepts rainfall, reducing infiltration and pore pressure. Limiting: (1) Deep-seated bedrock failures (planar slides along joints) occur below root zone. (2) Seismic shaking and toe erosion by rivers can override root reinforcement. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "yes, trees stop all landslides") shows oversimplification of failure mechanisms and scale mismatch.

questions.q: Design a field observation checklist for a student team visiting a slopes in the Nilgiris to distinguish between active creep, dormant earthflow, and recent landslide scars. Include at least five observable features with the process each indicates.
questions.a: Checklist: (1) Pistol-butt trees / tilted poles → creep. (2) Hummocky, lobate terrain with intact vegetation → dormant earthflow. (3) Fresh, steep head scarp with exposed bedrock and debris tongue → recent landslide. (4) Tension cracks parallel to slope → incipient landslide/earthflow. (5) Soil texture: clay-rich, plastic → earthflow potential; coarse, blocky → landslide potential. A poor checklist (e.g., only "look for cracks") misses diagnostic morphology and material clues.
